title: The Semester of the band room
premise: Theo Fairweather has spent senior year keeping their head down, raising siblings Marisol and Dev while Mom works hospital nights, and counting the days to graduation. When a group chat called 'the band room' begins posting predictions that come true—pop quiz questions, a bus crash averted, a teacher's resignation—Theo realizes the chat's members are somehow tapping the town's oldest tradition: the Founders' Day march the marching band plays before every home game. But the school board, led by a superintendent hungry for state funding, plans to end the tradition and sell the band room's century-old archive. As the predictions grow darker and more personal, Theo discovers they are the chat's unwitting anchor—their grandmother's sheet music holds the memory the town keeps forgetting. To save the tradition before the last game of the season, Theo must choose between the anonymity that kept their family safe and stepping into the light as the keeper of the town's memory. In the finale, the band plays the lost march at the last game, the board relents under public pressure, and Theo finally lets themselves be seen—by the town, and by Priya, the bandmate who saw them first.
about_author: Tamsin Nakamura is a former high school marching band section leader who grew up in a rust-belt town where Friday night football was the closest thing to a civic religion. She writes stories about kids holding families together and towns holding secrets.

chapters.title: Attendance Is Mandatory
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A morning of packing lunches, forging a permission slip for Dev, and slipping into class late establishes the weight Theo carries. The emotional beat: exhausted competence masking resentment about graduation feeling like a prison release date.

chapters.title: The Group Chat Nobody Made
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Seven students find themselves added to a chat named 'the band room' with no creator. The first message predicts tomorrow's fire drill to the minute. Beat: uneasy curiosity, the thrill of being chosen.

chapters.title: Pop Quiz
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The chat predicts a chemistry quiz word-for-word; Theo refuses to use it but can't unsee it. At home, Marisol asks why Theo never does anything fun. Beat: guilt over wanting more than duty allows.

chapters.title: Sectionals
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Rehearsal introduces the band's fragile ecosystem and Mr. Okafor's reverence for the Founders' Day march no one else remembers. Priya notices Theo watching the old sheet music cabinet like it's a door. Beat: first spark between them.

chapters.title: The Bus on Route 9
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The chat warns of a brake failure; Theo breaks invisibility to pull the alarm, delaying the team bus. They're hailed a hero and hate it. Beat: the cost of being seen begins.

chapters.title: Superintendent Voss
chapters.summary: Mr. Okafor's POV. Voss tours the band room, eyeing the archive, hinting that arts funding depends on 'modernization.' He mentions the march is 'historically insignificant.' Beat: quiet menace; power sizing up what it will take.

chapters.title: What Grandma Left in the Flute Case
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Cleaning out storage, Theo finds their late grandmother's handwritten march score annotated with dates—dates matching the chat's predictions. Beat: dread braided with wonder; memory as inheritance.

chapters.title: Seven Strangers, One Chat
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The seven members meet secretly in the actual band room and compare notes: each received a fragment of the march's melody in a dream. Beat: tentative alliance, the warmth of shared strangeness.

chapters.title: Homecoming, Predicted
chapters.summary: Dev's POV (first sibling chapter). The chat predicts homecoming will flood; Theo dismisses it, then spends the dance night bailing water at the gym with Priya while the kids wait home alone. Beat: Theo's two worlds colliding, badly.

chapters.title: Voss Proposes a Vote
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The board announces the tradition ends after this season; the archive goes to a private buyer. Okafor is suspended for 'curriculum irregularities.' Beat: righteous anger curdling into fear.

chapters.title: The Prediction That Was Wrong
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. For the first time, a prediction fails—and the chat goes silent for three days. Theo realizes the accuracy depends on someone playing or remembering the march. Beat: hope inverted into responsibility.

chapters.title: Marisol Knows Something
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol admits she's been humming the march for weeks—she found Grandma's cassette. She's been feeding fragments into her own dreams. Beat: Theo's protectiveness clashes with awe at her sister's gift.

chapters.title: Detention with Mr. Okafor
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Suspended but sneaking back, he tells Theo the truth: the march was written by four founders, one of them a Fairweather, as an act of communal remembering after a plague year the town chose to forget. Beat: history as burden passed down.

chapters.title: The Bribe
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Voss offers Theo a full scholarship endorsement if they hand over the score and let the tradition die quietly. Money means college means freedom. Beat: temptation rendered honestly; love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: What Theo Almost Did
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya learns Theo met Voss and feels betrayed; she accuses Theo of choosing escape again. Their fight cracks open Theo's real fear—that being known means being needed forever. Beat: heartbreak as honesty.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. A fire guts the band room overnight; the chat's final prediction arrives too late to stop it. Only items saved: Grandma's score, smuggled out days earlier by Marisol. Beat: grief, suspicion of arson, stakes made physical.

chapters.title: Who Set the Fire
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Evidence points to a janitor paid through a shell company tied to Voss's donor. Theo must decide whether exposing it means testifying publicly—as the kid from the group chat, by name. Beat: the point of no return.

chapters.title: Rehearsal in the Parking Lot
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. With no band room, the students rehearse the reconstructed march in the parking lot at dawn; half the town stops to listen. Beat: the community remembering itself; Theo and Priya reconcile over shared music.

chapters.title: The Last Game of the Season
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Climax. Before kickoff, with Voss threatening to cut the power, the band plays the Founders' Day march acapella as the stands rise to sing words they didn't know they remembered. Beat: triumph through collective memory.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Okafor's POV. Theo testifies at the emergency board meeting, score in hand, naming names. Voss resigns; the archive is preserved and the tradition codified. Beat: justice without euphoria—cost acknowledged.

chapters.title: Graduation Day
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Theo walks across the stage having stopped counting days. The chat dissolves itself, its purpose complete. Priya and Theo make plans that assume a future together. Beat: release; duty transformed into chosen love.

chapters.title: Coda: The March Continues
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. One year later, Marisol leads the band as drum major, teaching freshmen the march. Theo visits from college, carrying lunch for the little ones out of habit, then out of joy. Beat: memory kept alive by choice, not obligation.
